column2: On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the Messenger of Allah (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace) said:

“If people were given according to their claims, men would claim the wealth and the blood of others. But the burden of proof is on the claimant, and the oath is on the one who denies.” A ḥasan hadith, reported by al-Bayhaqī and others in this way; part of it is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs.

Bi-daʿwāhum (“according to their claims”): merely on their statement before a judge that others owe them some right, “men would claim”: men are mentioned specifically because that is usually their concern.
“The blood of men and their wealth”: so that the defendant would be unable to protect his life and wealth.
Al-muddaʿī (“the claimant”): one who asserts something hidden that is contrary to the apparent state of affairs.
“And the oath is on the one who denies”: because the default is that he is free of liability for what is demanded of him, and he holds to that.
No one is to be judged in favour of merely on his claim.
It is not permissible to judge except by what the Sharīʿah has laid down, even if the claimant's truthfulness seems most likely.
The oath is on the defendant in all cases.
